title: Correct attribution drift when API key rotation + sub-account merges affect quota and rate-limit ownership
creator: Priya Shah
description:
Summary: Some customers report unexpected quota exhaustion and rate-limit errors after API key rotation or when sub-accounts were merged. Investigation shows usage tokens were attributed to the wrong workspace/org in certain races between the key-rotation handler and the attribution cache invalidation. This resulted in billing miscounts and abrupt quota blocks for the rightful owners.

Reproduction steps observed in logs: 1) Customer rotates master API key A -> new key B. 2) Concurrent requests continue flowing with key A while the key-rotation event triggers internal mapping updates and a sub-account merge job runs. 3) The attribution cache (workspace_by_key) uses a stale mapping for a short window; newly ingested usage rows are stamped with the old workspace id but later metadata changes merge that workspace into a different billing owner. 4) Downstream aggregation (hourly-rollups) uses the final merged owner mapping but some intermediate enforcement components (rate limiter, per-key quota check) had used the transient mapping, causing double-counting or attributing usage to the wrong tenant.

Observed consequences: - Incorrect per-org quotas triggered (customers hit quota despite available allowance). - Billing invoices that include usage from merged child accounts assigned incorrectly. - Rate-limit enforcement applied inconsistently across requests leading to customer-facing errors.

Hypothesis / root cause: We discovered two correlated issues: 1) The attribution lookup path is duplicated across components (ingest, enforcement, rollup), and only the rollup pipeline subscribes to the canonical key->workspace change feed. 2) Key rotation and sub-account merge events are not processed atomically with respect to attribution cache invalidation. Race windows allow requests to be processed with stale mapping while downstream state mutates.

Proposed fix: 1) Change attribution to be authoritative and centralized: introduce a single service endpoint (auth-attribution) that returns the canonical workspace/org for a given API key and guarantees eventual consistency by applying rotation and merge events synchronously for a brief window. Components will consult this endpoint for enforcement and ingestion instead of local caches. 2) Short-term mitigation: on key-rotation events, publish a typed invalidation message that enforcement components listen to and block for up to 2s to allow mapping reconciliation (configurable). 3) Backfill: run a reconciliation job to re-attribute suspect usage rows over the last 30 days where rotation/merge events occurred in the same hour. Generate a correction report and credit affected customers. 4) Add telemetry: metric tagged by resolution-state (stale-cache-hit), error-rate bump at rotation windows, and a dashboard for quick triage.

Testing and validation: - Unit tests for attribution endpoint and cache TTL behavior. - Integration tests that simulate concurrent rotation + requests and assert enforcement decisions match rollup attribution. - Staging run of backfill on synthetic dataset followed by a small-scope production dry-run (no billing changes) to validate mapping diffs.

Rollout plan: 1) Deploy authoritative attribution endpoint behind a feature flag to enforcement and ingestion components (canary 10% of traffic). 2) Monitor stale-cache-hit and quota-failure metrics for 24h. 3) Ramp to 100% if stable. 4) Run backfill and apply credits for confirmed misattribution windows.

Rollback plan: revert enforcement callers to local caches; abort backfill if correction diffs exceed 0.5% of total usage in the window.

Risks and trade-offs: - Central API adds a new dependency and latency (~1-3ms p95). We'll mitigate with local read-through caches with short TTL and circuit breakers. - Backfill may require careful ordering to avoid double-crediting; include idempotency keys.
